title: Christmas Pudding
subtitle: Traditional steamed British Christmas pudding with dried fruit and brandy
excerpt: A dense, dark steamed pudding packed with dried fruit soaked in brandy, treacle, and warming spices. Made weeks ahead and resteamed on Christmas Day, then flamed at the table.

recipe.sourceNotes: Christmas pudding (also called plum pudding, though it contains no plums; the word was once used for dried fruit generally) has been a centrepiece of the British Christmas since the Victorian era, when Charles Dickens's description of the flaming pudding in A Christmas Carol cemented its cultural significance. The tradition of making the pudding on Stir-Up Sunday (the last Sunday before Advent) is based on the old Church of England collect for that day and the practical need for the pudding to be made at least a month in advance to mature. The high alcohol content and long steaming meant the pudding would keep for months, even years. The custom of hiding a silver coin in the pudding dates to Victorian times; a silver sixpence brought good fortune to whoever found it.

recipeTools.notes: A large pot with a lid, for steaming. A 1.2-litre pudding basin.

content.text: Soak the fruit overnight in the brandy: this is not optional. Cover the pudding basin tightly with a double layer of greaseproof paper and foil, tied with string; steam must not get in during the long cook. The water level must be kept topped up throughout steaming: check every 30 minutes. To reheat on Christmas Day, steam for a further 2 hours. To flame, warm a ladle of brandy, set it alight, pour over the pudding, and bring to the table while still burning.
The day before: mix all the dried fruit with the brandy in a large bowl. Cover and leave to soak overnight.

The next day, add all remaining ingredients to the soaked fruit. Stir thoroughly until combined. Have everyone in the family stir and make a wish. Butter a 1.2-litre pudding basin. Pack the mixture in firmly. Cover with a double layer of greaseproof paper and foil, tied securely with string.

Place in a large pot. Pour boiling water to come halfway up the sides. Cover and steam for 6 hours, topping up with boiling water every 30 to 45 minutes. Cool completely. Rewrap in fresh paper and store in a cool dark place for at least 2 weeks, or up to 3 months. On Christmas Day, steam for a further 2 hours before serving.
